opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few things. Obviously the Bay Area is still the center of gravity — the density of people working on frontier models there is just unmatched, and you can bump into someone at a coffee shop who's training the next big thing. I don't want to pretend Singapore replaces that.

But Singapore has some real advantages. One is the time zone. If you're part of a distributed team, being in Asia means you can work somewhat asynchronously. You hand things off, you run experiments while the US is asleep, and you get some deep-focus hours without a constant stream of pings. I actually found that quite productive.

The second is the talent pool in the region. There are a lot of very strong engineers and researchers in Asia — Singapore, but also people who'd happily relocate from around Southeast Asia, China, India — who don't necessarily want to move to the US, or can't easily because of visas. So Singapore becomes a nice hub where you can build a strong team without everyone having to go through the US immigration process.

Third, honestly, quality of life. It's safe, it's efficient, the food is great, and it's home for me. And the government is quite supportive of AI. There's a lot of interest in building up the ecosystem and they're pretty pragmatic about it.

The downside is the ecosystem is smaller. There's less of that serendipitous exchange of ideas, fewer people pushing the frontier locally, so you have to be more intentional about staying plugged in. You fly to SF a lot, you stay on Twitter, you keep in touch with folks. But I think for building a focused, high-quality team, Singapore is underrated.

r001.rationale: The response mentions asynchronous work and staying connected online, but does not say global connectivity makes physical location less important for interacting with the AI community.

r002.rationale: It describes time-zone flexibility and intentional efforts to stay plugged in, but does not explain that Singapore lets someone choose how immersed they are in the AI community.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I get asked this a lot, actually, because I spent a long time at Google in Mountain View and then I came back to start Reka here. And I think the honest answer is that it's a bit of a mixed bag, but there are real advantages that people underrate.

The first thing is talent density is actually pretty good here, it's just a different kind. Singapore has strong universities, NUS, NTU, and a lot of people who went abroad to do PhDs in the US and then come back, or want to come back, for family reasons or just because they like living here. So you get access to a pool of people who are quite strong technically but who aren't being bid up by every lab in San Francisco at the same time. In the Bay Area, if you're a small startup, you're competing with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta for the same fifty people, and that's brutal. Here it's a bit less of a feeding frenzy.

The second thing is just the practical stuff. The government is very supportive of tech, the infrastructure is excellent, it's a very easy place to operate a company from. Immigration is relatively straightforward for people we want to bring in, which honestly is a bigger deal than it sounds, because a lot of great researchers can't easily get a US visa. And it's a good hub for Asia, so if you care about the region, the time zones, the proximity to talent in India, China, Vietnam, Indonesia, that all matters.

Now, the disadvantages are real too, and I don't want to pretend otherwise. The Bay Area has this ambient density of people who are all working on the same problems, and you just absorb information by having coffee with people. You hear what's working, what's not, what the latest tricks are, before anything gets written up. Singapore doesn't have that, or it has a much smaller version of it. You have to work harder to stay plugged in. I spend a lot of time on Twitter, honestly, partly for that reason.

And the other thing is ambition and risk tolerance. Singapore culturally is a bit more conservative. People are a bit more inclined to take the safe job. That's changing, I think, and I'd like to think companies like ours are part of changing it, but it's not San Francisco where everyone you meet is starting something.

So my view is, it's a legitimately good place to build, especially if you're pragmatic about it. We're a global company anyway, we have people in multiple locations. But I'd push back on the idea that you have to be in the Bay Area to do frontier work. You don't. The compute doesn't care where you are, and the ideas travel fast enough now.

r001.rationale: The candidate says you do not have to be in the Bay Area for frontier work because ideas travel fast enough now, conveying that location matters less for staying connected to AI developments.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes Singapore as having a smaller AI community and says staying plugged in takes more effort; it does not describe flexibility in choosing how immersed to be.

astra-6.text:
I think Singapore has some real advantages, especially if you already have a clear idea of what you want to work on. It’s a very international place, English is widely spoken, and it’s easy to connect with people across Asia. There’s also strong support for science and technology, which is helpful when you’re trying to build something over the long term.

The Bay Area has this incredible density of people working on AI. You can have a casual conversation and come away with a collaborator, an idea, or a connection to funding. That’s hard to replicate.

But I think there’s also value in having a little distance from that environment. You can focus on a research direction without feeling quite as much pressure to follow whatever everyone is excited about that week. So I wouldn’t say Singapore is better across the board. It’s a different tradeoff: you give up some of that density, but you can have a very good base for doing focused work while staying connected internationally.

r001.rationale: The response says Singapore is international and that one can stay connected, but does not say global connectivity makes physical location less important for interacting with the AI community.

r002.rationale: It describes Singapore as offering distance from the Bay Area’s AI environment while still allowing international connection, enabling focused work with less immersion in its day-to-day pressures.

sol-6.1.text:
I think Singapore has a lot going for it. There’s strong technical talent, good universities, and it’s a place where people from across the region can come together. It’s also a very comfortable place to live, which matters when you’re thinking about where to build a team over the long term.

The Bay Area has this incredible density of researchers, founders, and capital. Singapore’s advantage is a little different: you can build a team with a strong connection to Asia and bring in perspectives that might be less represented in that ecosystem. I wouldn’t say one place is universally better. It depends on the people you want to work with and what you’re trying to build.
